newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - India flower sales bloom despite bottlenecks.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - India flower sales bloom despite bottlenecks.

text.p: The weather gods are kind and buyers are willing. Despite hurdles, India's flower exporters are pushing ahead in a quest to grab a big share of a global market worth billions of dollars.

But ailing infrastracture and bureaucratic red tape are standing in the way of the southern Indian city of Bangalore as it tries to put itself on the world flower map, aided by a moderate climate that helps perenial flower farming.
"We still don't have a cold storage in the airport," said Karuturi Ramakrishna, an executive of the South India Floriculture Association (SIFA).

Still, around 20 flower export firms, mainly selling roses, feel they have come a long way since their industry got off the ground three years ago, nurtured by India's six-year-old economic reforms that encouraged exports.
GROWTH DESPITE HURDLES
Businessmen looking at the past two years of growth believe it is only a question of time before they achieve their billion-dollar dreams.

Flower exports out of Bangalore, which accounts for most of the country's sales, are estimated to have topped 350 million rupees ($9.7 million) in 1996/97 (April-March), a seven-fold rise from 50 million rupees in 1995/96, Ramakrishna said.
In 1997/98, exports are expected to leap to 1.05 billion rupees ($28 milllion).
The western city of Pune, and to some extent the northern states of Punjab and Haryana, also serve as flower export centres.
In a global flower market estimated at around $40 billion a year, roses account for $7 billion to $8 billion. Bangalore firms say they can easily compete with current leaders Kenya and Israel.

"India's credibility is slowing coming up," Ranjan Pathak, a representative of Germany's Strumen Blumenhandel (SBH), one of the world's leading flower auction houses, told Reuters. SBH opened an office in Bangalore last year.
LOOKING FOR CRITICAL MASS

Exporters have tackled freight problems, launched an auction house to encourage local demand, identified new global buyers and established ties with government officials to ease bottlenecks at Bangalore's airport.
Individual growers now send 20,000 stems per shipment. If growers get together and shipments rise to 200,000 stems, European markets will offer more attractive bulk prices.
"It will be a purchase manager's delight," Ramakrishna said.
State-run Karnataka Agro Industries Corporation (KAIC) offered an umbrella of support to growers earlier this month (May) by launching exports under a common brand name, Nandi.
Acreage under flowers in the area is expected to grow to 75 hectares (185 acres) within a year from the current 55 hectares (135 acres)

Three years ago there was no freight space available in the cargo aircraft. Today, Air France, Kuwait Airways and KLM offer cargo space for flowers to Europe from Bangalore or through Bombay on four weekdays.
"Each airline was assured (by growers) of cargo space. We were able to produce the critical mass," Ramakrishna said.
But flowers face problems in the February-March season, when air cargo operators prefer the heavier textile cargo headed for Europe's summer sales.
The textile rush coincides with the Valentine's Day season, when Bangalore's flowers, which usually fetch 10 rupees (27 cents) a stem in Europe, can get as much as 25 rupees.
AIR CHARTERS THE ANSWER

Flower exporters are hoping for a state-supported charter for perishables to ease the bottleneck, which they say is critical because exporters realise 80 percent of their annual revenue in 20 percent of the business days.
"We have come a long way in terms of cargo space," Ramakrishna said. "But the demand-supply gap is growing."

During the peak season between December and March, there is a demand for 40 tonnes of cargo space a day, some 10 to 15 tonnes more than the availability. But profits are still hit because of the cargo bottleneck.
To get around the bottleneck, Bangalore's exporters decided to spread out their markets, until recently limited to the Netherlands, the world's main flower trading centre.

Exporters are looking at Japan, where return gifts for Valentine's Day -- February 14 -- are given in March, and towards Australia, which needs flowers during its winter months in July and August. Other markets like Singapore, Taiwan, Middle East and Korea are also being tapped.
"The earlier focus on Holland, Holland and more Holland has changed completely," Ramakrishna said.

But a cold storage at Bangalore's airport is still not ready as authorities have not given a promised piece of land near the tarmac, although state-run Agricultural Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) has approved a 7.5 million rupee ($210,000) grant to build the cold storage.
RED TAPE PROBLEMS
While the storage has been delayed by red tape, exporters have also had to cope with security regulations that forbid air-conditioned flower trucks from reaching airport tarmacs.

Customs regulations require cargo to be handed over hours before flights take off, and this has led to an erosion of quality, which can result in a loss of 10 to 20 percent of sale prices, Ramakrishna said.
Thanks to growing industries centred around coffee and computer software, Bangalore has become a world centre, but a much awaited international airport has been held up.

A consortium of Singapore's Changi Airport Authority and India's Tata group is ready to build the airport on a build-own-operate (BOO) basis, but officials in New Delhi are having second thoughts on whether it should be a build-operate-transfer (BOT) project.
Flower exporters say such confusion can prove costly. They say a global market is theirs for the taking if only direct cargo flights and better infrastructure could be organised.
